# why logic? {.divider}

We reason to persuade someone to accept a claim on the basis of something they
already accept.

::: {.notes}
One minute. The point of the opening puzzles is that they are cases where you
already reason well — the course is about making explicit what you are doing.
:::

## A coin toss

> You and I toss a coin, but we have no access to the other's coin. We each
> make a guess as to the outcome of the other's coin. We win if **at least one
> of us** makes a correct guess. We may agree on a common strategy before the
> coins are tossed.
>
> What strategy guarantees a win, no matter how the coins land?

. . .

Nothing about the two coins is correlated. So how can we guarantee anything?

::: {.notes}
Let them sit with it. Take a show of hands on whether a guaranteed strategy
exists at all before revealing that it does. The illustration at
coinflips.com.au is worth two minutes if the room is stuck.
:::

## A strategy that always wins

::: {.incremental}
- I make my guess **match** the outcome of my coin.
- You make your guess **differ** from the outcome of your coin.
:::

. . .

::: {.aside}
Take a moment: why does this work?
:::

::: {.notes}
Draw it on the chalkboard here — press C and sketch the two cases, MATCH and
DIFFER. Do not put the reconstruction up until someone has said the key thing:
the two cases are exhaustive.
:::

## Why it works

Once we toss our coins, they either match or they do not.

. . .

If they **match**, my guess is guaranteed to succeed — your coin landed exactly
as mine did.

. . .

If they **do not match**, your guess is guaranteed to succeed — your coin
landed differently from mine.

. . .

Either way, one of our guesses succeeds, and we win.

## The same case, made explicit {.smaller}

::: {.argument}
::: {.incremental}
1. Either the outcomes of our tosses match or they do not.
2. If they match, then since I guess the outcome I observed in my coin, I am
   guaranteed to succeed.
3. If I succeed, then at least one of us does, and we win.
4. If they do not match, then since you guess a different outcome from the one
   you observed, you are guaranteed to succeed.
5. If you succeed, then at least one of us does, and we win.
:::

::: {.conclusion .fragment}
6. So at least one of us succeeds, and we win the game.
:::
:::

::: {.notes}
This is the slide the whole opening builds to. Reveal one premise at a time and
leave them all up: the argument has to be visible *as a whole* for the last step
to land. Ask before revealing 6: what is still missing? (Nothing — that is the
point.)
:::

# arguments {.divider}

From a body of statements — the **premises** — to a statement they are meant to
support — the **conclusion**.

## Premises and conclusion

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="46%"}
> A gift card is better than a postcard. A postcard is better than nothing.
> Therefore, a gift card is better than nothing.
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.fragment}
**Premises**

1. A gift card is better than a postcard.
2. A postcard is better than nothing.

::: {.conclusion}
**Conclusion**, marked by 'therefore'

3. A gift card is better than nothing.
:::
:::
:::
:::

::: {.notes}
Contrast with the companion case: "A gift card is better than nothing. Nothing
is better than a yacht. So a gift card is better than a yacht." Same shape,
absurd result — worth putting on the board by hand rather than on a slide.
:::

## Definition

::: {.argument}
An **argument** is a sequence of declarative sentences, the **premises**, and a
declarative sentence marked as the **conclusion**.
:::

. . .

We use *declarative* sentences to make statements, which are true or false.
Contrast *interrogative* and *imperative* sentences, which ask and command.

. . .

::: {.aside}
There is no fixed order. 'So', 'thus', 'therefore', 'it follows that' mark the
conclusion wherever it appears.
:::

## Extracting an argument from a paragraph

> Time travel is impossible. For if time travel were possible, then a time
> traveler could change the past. Nothing, however, can change the past.

. . .

Which sentence is the conclusion?

. . .

::: {.argument}
1. If time travel were possible, then a time traveler could change the past.
2. Nothing can change the past.

::: {.conclusion}
3. [Time travel is impossible.]{.cardinal}
:::
:::

::: {.notes}
The conclusion comes *first* here, and 'for' marks what supports it. This is the
skill they will need all term. If there is time, do Argument B from the notes on
the chalkboard the same way.
:::

# validity {.divider}

Some arguments are *risk-free*: the truth of the premises guarantees the truth
of the conclusion.

## Which of these are risk-free? {.smaller}

::: {.incremental}
> Whales live underwater. Few mammals live underwater. Therefore, whales are not
> mammals.

> People are now carrying umbrellas on the street. Therefore, it must be
> raining.

> *All Things Considered* is a radio program. All radio programs are broadcast
> at least once a week. So *All Things Considered* is broadcast at least once a
> week.

> No one carries an umbrella on the street unless it is raining. Someone is now
> carrying an umbrella on the street. Therefore, it is raining.
:::

::: {.notes}
Two of the four. Take a vote on each as it appears, before saying anything.
The umbrella pair is the useful contrast: same subject matter, different form.
:::

## Risk-free because of a pattern

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
> If there is gas in the tank, the engine will start. There is gas in the tank.
> So the engine will start.

::: {.fragment}
::: {.argument}
1. If $p$, then $q$
2. $p$

::: {.conclusion}
3. Therefore, $q$
:::
:::
:::
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
> Either the butler did it or the gardener did it. The butler did not do it. So
> the gardener did it.

::: {.fragment}
::: {.argument}
1. $p$ or $q$
2. Not $p$

::: {.conclusion}
3. Therefore, $q$
:::
:::
:::
:::
:::

::: {.fragment .aside}
$p$ and $q$ are placeholders for English declarative sentences. The pattern never
takes you from true premises to a false conclusion — whatever they stand for.
:::

## Validity

::: {.argument}
An argument is **valid** if, and only if, it is an instance of a **valid
argument form**.
:::

::: {.incremental}
1. A valid argument form has *no* instances with true premises and a false
   conclusion.
2. A valid argument form preserves truth regardless of subject matter.
:::

. . .

::: {.aside}
So to show a form **invalid**, it is enough to produce one instance with true
premises and a false conclusion.
:::

## One instance is enough {.smaller}

::: {.argument}
1. $p$ if, and only if, $q$

::: {.conclusion}
2. $p$ and $q$
:::
:::

. . .

::: {.argument}
1. Mark Twain wrote *Hamlet* if, and only if, Samuel Clemens did.

::: {.conclusion}
2. Mark Twain wrote *Hamlet* and Samuel Clemens did.
:::
:::

. . .

::: {.aside}
The premise is **true** — Mark Twain *is* Samuel Clemens. The conclusion is
**false** — neither wrote *Hamlet*. One such instance kills the form.
:::

::: {.notes}
Insist on this: we did not need to survey every instance. One suffices. That
asymmetry between showing validity and showing invalidity runs through the
whole course.
:::
